To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

members of disadvantaged groups are more likely to perceive the ingroup's relative worth to be lower than that of the outgroup when they perceive the ingroup to be negatively evaluated by members of the dominant outgroup (Study 1), and that this effect is mediated by perceived societal unfairness (Study 2).

(a) perceived negativity of a dominant out-group (meta-stereotypes) is related to lower perceived group-worth relative to that group; and (b) perceived negativity of dominant out-groups is related to lower views about societal fairness, which in turn is related to lower ingroup relative worth.

members of disadvantaged groups who are concerned that members of the dominant group are prejudiced towards their ingroup have more negative views about societal fairness and, in turn, lower perceived group worth.

the implications of perceived outgroup negativity for members of disadvantaged groups and suggests that such negativity may be a barrier to their social mobility.

we are not likely to get past the glass-ceilings that are holding us back from reaching equality in our society, and that is because of the meta-stereotypes that are holding us down and preventing us from moving forward.

members of disadvantaged groups may be more likely to perceive their group as being worth less than the outgroup if they are concerned about the outgroup's negative views of their group.
members of disadvantaged groups are likely to be less motivated to pursue upward mobility if they believe that the dominant outgroup perceives them negatively and that society is unfair to them.
